---
title: "Practical: evidence for tissue identity and function"
---

## Question and preparation

What observations justify naming a tissue, and how does that tissue help an
organ work? Work in pairs, then submit one individual
observation sheet. You need paper and a pencil; the cases below supply textual
observations. They are deliberately constructed descriptions, **not microscope
images or records of actual specimens**. This activity practises reasoning
before a specimen session; passing it does not establish visual identification
or dissection skill. Those require the course's actual slides, atlas and
instructor-led practical.

Review the four broad tissue categories: epithelium forms linings and
interfaces; connective tissue supports and links structures; muscle generates
force; nervous tissue supports information processing and transmission.
Actual organs contain several categories. A kidney section is not a single
homogeneous tissue.

## A reproducible observation record

For each case record: the features explicitly supplied; the most defensible
tissue class; two features supporting it; a likely function; one plausible
alternative; and an observation that would discriminate between the two.
Keep observation separate from inference. “Several layers of cells” is an
observation; “protects against abrasion” is a functional interpretation.
Do not infer a named organ from a common epithelial shape alone.

### Station 1: interfaces

**Case A:** a continuous lining appears one cell thick. Cells are flattened,
and nuclei interrupt an otherwise thin barrier. A capillary is immediately
adjacent; no thick keratin layer is described.

**Case B:** a lining contains several cell layers. Surface cells are flattened.
Deeper cells appear less flattened. The tissue borders a surface exposed to
friction.

**Case C:** a tubular profile has a single layer of approximately cube-shaped
cells around a lumen. Nuclei are central. Other sections show many similar
tubules, but no specialised border can be resolved.

1. Classify the epithelia by layer number and surface-cell shape.
2. Explain why A is compatible with exchange and B with protection. Do not
   claim every thin lining has the same transport properties.
3. Could C establish “kidney” on its own? Name an additional contextual
   feature you would ask to inspect.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

“Simple” and “stratified” describe layers; “squamous”, “cuboidal” and
“columnar” describe cell shape. Function also depends on junctions,
membrane proteins and the surrounding structures.
:::

### Station 2: force and information

**Case D:** long parallel fibres show repeated transverse bands. Multiple
nuclei lie near fibre edges; fibres are not described as branching.

**Case E:** short branching fibres show transverse bands and central nuclei.
Distinct cell-to-cell junction regions are visible.

**Case F:** spindle-shaped cells each have a central nucleus. No transverse
bands are visible; bundles surround a hollow organ.

**Case G:** large cell bodies contain prominent nuclei and several processes;
many smaller supporting cells surround them. The description alone does not
specify which processes are axons or dendrites.

4. Identify the best broad tissue interpretation for each case, explaining
   the features rather than matching a keyword.
5. Which two cases are striated? Why is “striated means skeletal” insufficient?
6. Predict consequences of disrupting coordinated contraction in E and
   sustained contraction in F. Link the prediction to organ function, not
   diagnosis of a disease.

### Station 3: organ architecture

Sketch a cross-section of a generic transport tube with an inner lining,
connective support and a muscular layer. Label the lumen and identify which
side contacts the transported material. Explain how a change in muscular
diameter can alter flow. Then explain why a tube described this way cannot
be identified confidently as either a blood vessel or a gut segment without
further observations.

Draw a fish gill lamella and a mammalian alveolar interface as **conceptual
diagrams**, not replicas of slides. Mark the environmental medium, a thin
exchange barrier and blood. Write two common exchange requirements and one
important difference in ventilation or medium. A functional resemblance does
not establish the same evolutionary origin of every component.

## Turning descriptions into genuine visual practice

Use the institution's provided normal-tissue slides when available. For each
unknown, begin at low magnification, orient the tissue, then inspect selected
features at higher magnification under the local microscope instructions.
Record image/slide ID, magnification or scale bar, orientation and two
diagnostic observations. Distinguish sectioning angle from biological shape:
a longitudinal tube and its cross-section can look very different.

Do not invent a scale or copy an atlas label onto an uncertain feature. Return
to the specimen if two alternatives fit. A descriptive record with justified
uncertainty is better evidence than a confident name without observations.

## Completion check

Leave with the seven case records, two conceptual exchange diagrams and a
paragraph answering: “What extra evidence would I need before identifying an
unknown organ?” End by naming the visual skill this text exercise cannot
verify. Review representative tissue images through the linked learning
resources or the course atlas; no image-reuse rights are implied here.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Self-check

A: simple squamous; B: stratified squamous; C: simple cuboidal. D: skeletal
muscle; E: cardiac muscle; F: smooth muscle; G: nervous tissue. C's shape
alone cannot establish a kidney origin. The diagrams should show thin barriers
and large exchange area, while distinguishing water passing gills from air
ventilating lungs. These answers do not replace visual specimen assessment.
:::
